item.title: What's More Interesting—Swinging Balls or a Stranger's Face?
item.description:
Child Development

What's More Interesting—Swinging Balls or a Stranger's Face?

New research finds girls attend to faces more than boys within hours of birth.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Newborn girls averaging 33 hours old looked at faces more than boys who split attention evenly.
  • Measurable staring appeared immediately after birth, suggesting that genetics influences attention.
  • The study replicates a debated 2,000 study supporting the reality of predetermined sex differences.
Source: Google Gemini/AI image generator

Imagine you are a newborn. You are just a few hours old, cradled in your mother's arms on a hospital bed, and you know nothing about anything, except the world inside your mother's body. You cannot talk, crawl, or hold up your head. A researcher props a laptop in front of you and plays a short video. On one side of the screen, a woman's face smiles, blinks, and turns toward you. On the other side, a set of silver balls swing and click in a hypnotic, mechanical motion, the kind of toy that rests on your boss's desk. Nobody has told you which one matters more. You seem pragmatically clueless, but are you? Incredibly, groundbreaking research shows that what you do next depends partly on your biological sex.

The question that won't go away

Few debates have generated more controversy, and more inappropriate inferences, than the question of male/female behavioral differences. The typical rationale used to explain differences is "acculturation," which suggests that how children are raised determines what they like. Pink blankets for girls, blue ones for boys; dolls for girls, trucks for boys contribute to a lifetime of cultural preferences. No one disputes the influence of culture on intelligence, interest, and motivation. But when a difference in attention shows up when a baby has one day of experience, culture is not the answer to explain the difference.

That is exactly what Khan et al. (2026) addressed in their new study that revisits one of developmental psychology's most cited and most criticized experiments (Connellan et al., 2000). In that study, Connellan and colleagues found that newborn girls looked longer at a human face while newborn boys looked longer at a mechanical mobile (Connellan et al., 2000). That original study was hailed as evidence of built-in sex differences. However, the study was excoriated for its methods, which biased the experimenters. The researchers knew the sex of the infants in advance, a serious research error that doesn’t fly in today’s more sophisticated studies like the one by Khan et al. The 2000 results hadn’t been replicated until now.

What the new study did differently

Khan and colleagues recruited 130 healthy, full-term newborns from a hospital in Cambridge, UK, averaging just 33 hours old. Instead of a live person and a physical toy, every infant watched the same standardized video: a smiling, moving face on one half of the screen and a Newton's cradle, the swinging-balls desk toy, on the other. Three independent coders, blind to each baby's sex, timed exactly where and for how long each infant looked. The researchers even matched the two videos for size, brightness, and how much on-screen motion each contained, so a simple attraction to movement could not explain the results.

Girls looked at faces; boys looked at both

The pattern that emerged was distinctive. When looking, girls devoted significantly more time to faces than boys did. Measured in raw seconds, girls showed a clear preference for the face over the balls, while boys showed no preference either way, splitting their attention roughly evenly. Across the full sample, every newborn looked at the face more than chance would predict…faces are apparently as compelling at birth as they are to curious adults! Overall, girls had a stronger facial preference, and boys were comparatively even-handed between a person and the toy.

Nature, nurture, or chance?

I have spent a career arguing against tidy either-or (binary) explanations of human behavior, whether the subject is motivation or, as it is here, the origins of sex differences. This study reminds us why binary views or simple explanations of causality are rarely accurate. A newborn is not a blank slate, but the study is also not proof of pure biological determinism. Parents may already speak, gaze, and touch sons and daughters differently within the first hours of life, and prenatal and hormonal influences such as dopamine synthesis between male and female fetuses may shape brain development before either environment or culture has an impact. Girls, on average, also reach many developmental milestones slightly faster than boys in early life, so maturation itself could play a role. The honest answer, as usual, is not nature instead of nurture. It is nature setting a foundation that experience amplifies, represses, or redirects behavior.

Why a swinging toy matters to all of us

This is not about crib antics. Measuring when sex differences in attention first appear, and how much of those differences trace to biology rather than experience, gives us a better understanding of why girls and boys develop differently. If measurable differences in social orientation are present from birth, those differences may explain lifetime patterns of interaction without turning a modest average difference into a verdict on any individual baby, girl or boy. So, the next time you notice a pair of swinging silver balls and glance away toward an unfamiliar face, you may just be obeying wiring that was installed before your parents ever picked out the color of your first blankie!

item.title: I'm on a Communication Diet, and You Should Be Too
item.description:
Attention

I'm on a Communication Diet, and You Should Be Too

How to be fully human in the modern era.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Modern life has an ocean of content to consume.
  • Trying to consume all that interests you can leave you depleted and overwhelmed.
  • We all need to choose what we read/watch carefully and keep the amount low intentionally.
  • Doing so can leave us more alert and energetic for the other parts of life and no less informed.
Reading the paper while the brook flows by
Source: K. Bayzanur/Pexels

In this post, I am going to make an unusual and seemingly counterproductive recommendation for better mental health. I am going to recommend that you do fewer things that are interesting, informative, and entertaining.

But all these activities foster personal growth. Why would I suggest you do less of them? Read on as I explain.

What I’ll discuss here are the choices we must make to thrive in Western culture without falling victim to its excesses. The choices I have in mind are about things that educate, enlighten, interest, and entertain us. This will not be about major life choices such as our health, relationships and careers. As I think you’ll agree, we are now bombarded by content of all kinds that can leave us quite overwhelmed and psychologically unwell. We need a way of dealing with this without leaving quality content behind.

The solution is a practice of intentional simplicity. That will include electing not to pursue things that may enlighten, interest, inform, or entertain us. We can do this and still maintain our quality of life, personal development, and good citizenship.

To better understand this, let’s look at some recent human history: how dietary habits changed during the 1950s, 60s, and 70s. For all human history prior to those decades, there was never an excess of food. Food always existed on the edge of scarcity. No one worried about eating too much or even eating the wrong things. Just eating was enough to worry about.

But in the decades mentioned above, something happened that has never been the case in human history. There was an excess of food throughout Western culture. You could live comfortably, have a full belly, and do virtually no exercise. This combination made for some very unhealthy people.

The conclusion of the medical establishment and the citizens of Western society was that they had to eat less and choose what they ate more carefully. That seems completely normal to us now, but considered in the grand sweep of history, it was a remarkable and unprecedented change. What I propose is similar but instead of food, it deals with certain facets of our mental life. What’s at stake is our emotional well-being.

We are currently bombarded with choices in all forms of information and expression. The internet has caused an explosion of articles, videos, blogs, and podcasts that make the printing press look like a small increment in production. Ideas, counter-ideas, and counter-counter-ideas now exist for every corner of human experience. We must make serious attempts to prune the investment of our attention just as we carefully choose how much and what we eat.

Let’s begin with an example from the news. This may be a newspaper, social media, podcast or wherever you get your news. Imagine you see an article whose headline is: a politician you know has voted in favor of a policy you endorse. Normally, you might open and read the article, but judging from the headline, you’re probably not going to learn more than what the headline and subtitle stated. You’ll likely learn some details which you will quickly forget. There will be other examples in your news source that may look just as interesting on the surface, perhaps entertaining or novel.

Our society is awash in sources of communication and entertainment. Cities are buzzing with opinions, artistic expression, and new experiences. Going down each rabbit hole will deteriorate your attention as you’re spending it on making your way through this tangle of words and images rather than benefiting from it.

Attention is not something we have an infinite amount of. It is very much like energy. You only have so much and when you spend it, it’s gone. If you spend too much of it over a long period of time, the chronic deficit will cause some damage. This may be a stress related illness such as migraines, irritable bowel disease, fatigue, or hypertension; or more commonly psychological effects on your mood, level of tension, relationships, and overall sense of well-being. On a deeper level, your vulnerability to mental disorders such as depression goes up significantly.

There is certainly nothing wrong with delving into interesting articles. In fact, you may benefit and enjoy all of them. The important thing, and the point here, is that the communication world is now an ocean of such articles. You could spend your entire day with one news source going through perfectly interesting or entertaining articles. But we now live in a different world. Rather than dive into everything that piques our interest, we must make decisions and actively curtail these efforts.

Now, when I read the paper, I look over a group of articles and decide which are most likely to inform me about something important or show me content that is entertaining or new. Out of perhaps 10 articles I look at I will read only one or two. And even those I may read just the beginning because that’s where the basic information is.

The pruning process is twofold. First, I am deciding which information sources are likely to truly increase my knowledge and understanding (or entertain). Second, I am simply choosing fewer sources irrespective of their potential value. So better sources and less content overall is the goal to take an active role in simplifying your life.

In addition to news articles, we could consider books, movies, streaming TV shows, new restaurants, and other examples of possible sources of novelty or interest. I would use the same decision process to prune all these down.

I still like new and interesting streaming TV, books, and news, but I choose carefully and put aside all but the most fulfilling. Even then, I still might put it aside just to keep things simple. I am on a communication diet, and you should be too.

This may sound like a formula for a boring life. A rule more fit for a monastery than modern life. It may also raise the question as to whether a simple life makes you simple-minded. Just like the food diet which leaves you with more energy than over-eating; the communication diet leaves you with a calmer mind that is not lost in the jungle of opinion and expression. It also opens the gates of your mind to wander, reflect, and calmly notice what and who is around you.

This should not be taken to the point of changing your quality of life. Each person will be different in how this works for them. Some, like me, value simplicity. Others enjoy the wilds of opinions and originality. The goals of better choosing and few choices overall remain the same, but the final product will be different for everyone. The effects of simplicity on a calmer and more open mind are really what we are looking for.

Life in our modern era has brought new and unexpected challenges to maintain our humanity. In an age of excess, simplification will be a bigger part of that effort. In any of these efforts, it is vital to understand that less is more. Our humanity will shine through if we do not obstruct it.

item.title: The Real Problem With Psychiatric Prescribing Is the Order
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Real Problem With Psychiatric Prescribing Is the Order

Some kids get the riskier drug first. Deprescribing should reverse that order.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Deprescribing has become a federal priority in 2026, via a February consensus and an HHS plan.
  • In a national cohort, half the youth started on antipsychotics for ADHD had not tried a stimulant first.
  • The fixable failure is sequencing: riskier drugs going in before safer, better-studied ones.

Psychiatry spent 2026 arguing about volume. In February, the American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology published a consensus statement on deprescribing psychotropic medications. In May, the Department of Health and Human Services announced an action plan to “curb psychiatric overprescribing.” The American Psychiatric Association answered that the bigger crisis is people who can’t get care at all.

I was interviewed for AAMCNews this month about where I land. Both sides are counting prescriptions. The data I’ve worked with for a decade point to a narrower variable that does more harm to children: which prescription comes first.

Half had never tried the first-line drug

In 2019, my colleagues and I published a national study in JAMA Network Open of 187,563 commercially insured young people, ages 3 to 24, newly diagnosed with ADHD between 2010 and 2015. We excluded anyone with a diagnosis for which antipsychotics are FDA-approved. Within a year, 2.6 percent had started an antipsychotic. Among those children, 47.9 percent had never filled a prescription for a stimulant, the first-line treatment for ADHD. Only 8.4 percent had tried both stimulant families, methylphenidate and amphetamine, before the antipsychotic.

That matters because the two drug classes carry very different risks. Antipsychotics can add several kilograms of weight in a few months and shift blood sugar and cholesterol in children. Stimulants have decades of trial data behind them and among the largest effect sizes in psychiatry.

As I told the reporter, what we were seeing is children receiving a more dangerous medication before a less dangerous one. That’s a sequencing problem. The question is rarely medication or no medication; it's whether we worked through the safer, better-studied options first.

Why the order goes wrong

Nobody sets out to skip steps, but the system pushes toward them. Visits are short, families want relief, and writing a prescription is the fastest help a clinician can offer. A month of a generic stimulant can cost less than a single therapy session. Parent training for ADHD works moderately well, but it’s a 15-week commitment that a family already stretched thin often can’t make without medication alongside it.

So I don’t take the side that says medication is the problem. I once treated a child in the emergency department who had jumped off a roof after stopping his ADHD medication. The right answer for him was combined treatment: Medication and behavioral work together, at the lowest dose that could do the job.

Deprescribing should run the sequence backward

If medications should go in from safest to riskiest, they should come off in reverse once the reason for them is gone. For a child with ADHD taking a stimulant and an antipsychotic, that usually means asking what the antipsychotic was for. If there’s no clear indication, it’s the first candidate to taper, slowly and one drug at a time. It also means checking whether the stimulant trial was ever adequate. One family at a low dose isn’t a trial, and optimizing the first-line drug often makes the second one unnecessary.

Volume is a poor proxy for harm. National dispensing data show stimulant use in children has been flat since 2011, and antipsychotic use has drifted down. A policy that simply aims for fewer prescriptions risks cutting off the children who are finally getting appropriate care, while leaving the order problem untouched.

If your child takes more than one psychiatric medication, bring four questions to the next appointment:

  • What was each one started for, and is that still true?
  • Was a stimulant tried at an adequate dose, and were both families tried?
  • When were weight, glucose, and cholesterol last checked?
  • And if we reduce something, which goes first, and why?

See the full numbers, including the age breakdown and the monitoring data, in a longer analysis on my site.

item.title: Connecticut Takes Key Step in Reforming Mental Health System
item.description:
Law and Crime

Connecticut Takes Key Step in Reforming Mental Health System

Pilot plan will offer vital mental health treatment instead of incarceration.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Connecticut has launched a pilot behavioral health court, focusing on treatment over incarceration.
  • A multidisciplinary task force aids in refining Connecticut's mental health court eligibility and services.
  • Early intervention in youth mental health can reduce arrests and improve outcomes.
Source: Katrin Bolovtsova / Pexels

This summer, Connecticut Supreme Court Chief Justice Raheem Mullins announced the state was piloting a specialized behavioral health court. Based in New Haven, it is intended to divert eligible individuals away from incarceration and into treatment under judicial supervision.

This work has the potential to provide critical assistance to thousands of individuals with mental health and substance use issues, all of whom are significantly overrepresented in the criminal justice system—our largest provider of mental health services. Fortunately, there are models throughout the country that have the ability to inform the direction of the program.

Existing Models of Behavioral Health Courts

In New York, where I practice as a family-focused mental health attorney, behavioral courts operate throughout the state and are integrated into a comprehensive problem-solving framework. Alternatively, California’s courts focus on connecting people with treatment and housing through a civil court process rather than criminal prosecution. Other states like Illinois, Texas, and Ohio have invested in and/or expanded their own specialized court systems, addressing various priorities based on the needs of their communities.

Connecticut’s pilot program will face similar decision-making. Crucially, it will need to determine eligibility, meaning whether the court will accept felony and/or misdemeanor defendants, repeat offenders, juveniles, and those who have been charged with domestic violence, sex offenses, and other crimes. In making such decisions, it will have to factor in community safety issues and its ability to deliver appropriate supportive housing and treatment resources.

Role of the Multi-Disciplinary Task Force

I’m heartened to see that Justice Mullins has assembled a multi-disciplinary task force to help think through these nuances. The complexity of behavioral and addiction issues requires the expertise of a broad range of professionals, specializing in fields spanning mental health law, psychiatry, social work, child welfare, law enforcement, criminal justice, and more.

Included in the task force is Connecticut Superior Court Judge Daniel Klau, who tragically lost his daughter to a fentanyl overdose in 2021. He brings the valuable perspective of a family member who knows firsthand what high-risk individuals and concerned loved ones facing these issues experience.

Such perspective is crucial given the roadblocks, gaps, and inequities that can limit the success of even the most well-designed behavioral health court systems. Research has consistently shown that these courts are most effective when they operate within communities that have robust Medicaid funding, supportive housing, crisis stabilization services, and accessible outpatient psychiatric care. This broader system of support is especially important for juveniles.

Importance of Early Intervention

Providing young people experiencing mental health crises with timely treatment and appropriate interventions, rather than relying primarily on punitive measures, can alter the course of their lives. In recent years, early intervention has been shown to reduce arrests, decrease negative interactions with law enforcement, and improve long-term outcomes, underscoring the importance of integrating youth-focused services into behavioral health court models.

Behavioral health courts represent a meaningful step toward a system of justice that balances accountability with compassion and evidence-based intervention. By diverting individuals away from prison, these courts connect people with the stability and treatment they need to break the cycle of crisis, hospitalization, and incarceration. Connecticut’s first behavioral health court presents an opportunity to embrace a model that has already helped thousands of people across the country. I am optimistic about what this pilot program can achieve in Connecticut and will watch its progress with great interest.

item.title: Betrayal: How to Heal the Brain and the Psyche
item.description:
Resilience

Betrayal: How to Heal the Brain and the Psyche

Betrayal is an injury to both brain and psyche. Successful healing involves both.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Recovering from betrayal can be challenging.
  • Betrayal represents and injury to the brain and the psyche.
  • Effective healing rests upon addressing both psychological and biological injuries.
Source: Moeinium / Pixabay

Sociobiologists tell us that human beings are hard-wired to live in groups, usually small groups of 10 to 12 people. For these groups to function effectively and be sustained over years, if not generations, there must be some degree of mutual attraction, trust amongst members, and some basic affiliative drive for interpersonal attachment. Something this important to the success of a species must therefore have a biological basis that is present at birth and that may then be shaped by experience.

In 1977, the seminal text Stress, Health, and the Social Environment: A Sociobiologic Approach to Medicine (Henry & Stephens, 1977) first described the physiological circuitry of just such a system. They called it “the cement of society” and argued it was as powerful a predictor of the success of the species as was the development of the prefrontal cortex (the basis for executive functions, rational thought, and raw intelligence). Imagine the implications of physiological injury to that affiliative drive. It is reasonable to believe the condition of interpersonal betrayal represents an injury not just to the psyche but also to the brain itself, causing disruption to intrapersonal and interpersonal well-being. Thus, there are two injuries, not just one. Healing from betrayal can be challenging, and this may be why. A common reason both self-help and professional therapies fail is that they fail to address both injuries. Here is a guide to healing both.

Betrayal

Betrayal is the violation of trust—an act in which someone violates faith, loyalty, a moral or performance expectation, or some implied or expressed agreement. To be considered betrayal, as opposed to more common acts of neglect or aggression, the violation must be perpetrated by a trusted partner, friend, caregiver, leader, employer, or institution.

The behavioral effects of betrayal include, but are not limited to, a syndrome similar to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD): loss of a sense of safety, hypervigilance, nightmares, intrusive memories and ruminations, reduced ability to trust others, anger, fear, numbing, depression, and a destruction of protective assumptions about the world (worldviews).

Disturbances to interpersonal behavior include avoidant attachment (withdrawal and isolation, difficulty forming healthy relationships, suspiciousness), anxious attachment (clinging to others, fear of abandonment), and a reduction in secure attachment sometimes characterized by self-sabotage.

Biologically, betrayal is best conceptualized as a biologic injury to the affiliative drive system. That system consists of (1) the anterior cingulate cortex (mediates social attraction, bonding, and empathy), (2) the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (regulates emotional responses and inhibits fear, enabling trust and affiliation), and (3) the hypothalamic pituitary circuit (releases oxytocin and vasopressin, neuropeptides central to social attachment).

The effects of betrayal appear to be (1) atrophy of the anterior cingulate cortex, thereby potentially reducing the drive for affiliation and bonding and perhaps interfering with empathy; (2) hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivation causing increased cortisol; (3) increased sympathetic nervous system tone (fight-or-flight response) associated with increased aggressiveness, fear, and hypervigilance; and (4) decreased oxytocin expression (the social bonding hormone), thus potentially weakening affiliative motivation. Lastly, betrayal appears to be capable of increasing perceptions of physical pain—thus, the notion of “heartache” may be as much physical as psychological (Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004).

The ruminations and even physiological reactions that constitute betrayal may become persistent through a mechanism of neuroplasticity. Simply said, the more one activates a particular brain region or circuit, the more likely that reaction and its underlying circuitry become the “default” behavioral pattern for everyday life.

Resilience and Growth in the Wake of Betrayal

The first step in resilience and growth after betrayal is to understand that it is a journey, not a destination achieved overnight.

The next step involves increasing the ability to self-regulate. Somatic therapies, mindfulness, meditation, and biofeedback are all effective interventions that can increase physiological self-control and begin to reset physiological dynamics (Everly & Lating, 2019).

Cathartic expression (emotional venting) begins to relieve both psychological and physical pressure. Catharsis can be through verbal expression, art therapy, writing an autobiography, and journaling.

Most important, however, is constructing a renaissance—a rebirth. An effective approach to achieve such a lofty goal is the four-step approach to building self-efficacy developed by Albert Bandura (1997). Start by observing others who can serve as role models. Next, construct a “to-do” list representing small successes that will lead you to your ultimate goal. Third, find a formal or informal coach or mentor who can provide objective feedback and encouragement. Lastly, practice daily exercises in self-regulation.

At the systems level, resilience and growth rest upon choosing leaders who possess three qualities: integrity, decisiveness, and an appreciation for the human side of the mission.

In Sum

It seems reasonable to conclude that betrayal injures the biologic systems that evolved to maintain human social cohesion. Early sociobiologists correctly identified the affiliative drive system as the biologic “cement of society,” and betrayal is a direct insult to that system. Recognizing betrayal as biologic injury reframes trauma theory, informs clinical practice, and deepens our understanding of organizational and community dynamics. Failure to do so perpetuates toxic organizational and societal cultures and erodes interpersonal support—which is the single best predictor of human resilience.

item.title: Thinking Is the New Luxury
item.description:
Cognition

Thinking Is the New Luxury

When answers are abundant, does thinking become scarce?

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI can hand us the answer, but it can't hand us the thinking that produced it.
  • Struggling with an idea changes you while a generated paragraph does not.
  • When everyone can fake the artifact, real thought starts to look like a luxury.
Source: Image by Johnnie Shannon from Pixabay.

Let's start with a history lesson.

There was a time when deep thinking was much more a luxury than a choice. Back then, being an intellectual required resources that were just unavailable—books, education, and, importantly, time itself. That time was typically defined by toil and the practical realities of living (not thinking) life. The luxury of thought was itself a type of privilege or even a royal indulgence.

Times have changed. Modernity has pushed against that reality as the education of society, in many instances, has become an important goal. Education became available, local libraries were built, and universities became accessible. And the internet shifted the scarcity of information to, what some call, a level of abundance. Thought, at least for the moment, had found itself.

Thinking didn't become easy; access to the substrate of thought became more accessible.

Today, I believe that artificial intelligence is causing an interesting "cognitive twist." in what thinking is and how we do it. Large language models provide something that resembles human thinking. But that might really be more of a perfected counterfeit of human thought itself. Now here's the twist: what once required intellectual effort can now be generated with much less of that effort.

We can increasingly fake the answer, but it's harder to fake the thinking.

Let's put this in some context. Of course, people have commonly borrowed ideas and presented concepts that were beyond their individual capacity. But I'll suggest that AI changes both the scale and sophistication of this. Today, AI allows us to offer something that looks remarkably like the "artifact of thought" without really experiencing the cognitive process itself that gets you there.

This is critically important because thinking itself does something—it changes the thinker. Struggling along the cognitive pathway to discovery is an essential part of how cognition develops. An answer can be transferred in an instant, but intellectual change that comes from traversing that path cannot.

This is what gave rise to what I call Activities of Daily Thinking. These are ordinary acts such as reading and writing (remember those?). They can seem almost trivial until AI makes them optional. Just as our physical capacities can decrease when we stop using them, cognitive capacities may depend partly on continuing to perform them.

This also aligns with something I've called the Abundance Bubble. AI is creating a sort of cognitive abundance—perhaps even an excess. Words and ideas are produced at a scale that was unimaginable just a few years ago. Interestingly, this newfound abundance can also create forms of scarcity. When intelligent output becomes ubiquitous, the human effort behind an idea may become harder to find. And paradoxically, more valuable.

In a world filled with polished cognitive artifacts, we may begin looking for different signals that thought actually occurred. A notebook filled with scribbles and revisions might just tell us something different from that perfect paragraph. So does the person who can explain how an idea developed. Even uncertainty might carry information because it reveals an engaged mind on a path of learning.

I have to admit, there's something that bothers me about turning thought into a status symbol. Thinking is something we should want to preserve broadly, for us all. It should never become a marker of privilege. But culture often assigns value to things once they become scarce—it's supply and demand. I wonder if sustained human thought may take on that kind of value in a world where its artifacts are abundant.

This is where Cognitive Sovereignty becomes important. It describes the ability to use AI while preserving, not relinquishing, our own human intellectual agency. And so, our history lesson comes full circle. Thought was once a luxury because a few people could actually afford to think. In the age of AI, it may become a luxury again because fewer of us will actually have to.

item.title: Cynics Who Are Gullible
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Cynics Who Are Gullible

The interesting case of "gullicism."

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Although gullibility and cynicism seem to be incompatible, there are many people who exhibit "gullicism."
  • Internet "trolls" are a good example of this, as are anti-vaxxers.
  • Gullicism helps to shed light on some of the potential dangers of artificial intelligence.

A cynic is someone who doubts the truth of many things generally believed to be true, while a gull is someone who accepts the truth of many things generally believed to be false. On the surface, these seem to be incompatible, but they share two tendencies: (a) a need to take a contrarian position, typically as part of a circle of other contrarians, and (b) a lack of openness to the possibility that one might be mistaken. This explains how someone could be cynical about some things while gullible about other things, as the person may choose to believe or disbelieve assertions based not on evidence but on how they feel about their source or content.

The word “gullicism” was coined to describe gullible cynics by Adam Serwer. In a March 2026 piece in The Atlantic titled "Gullible, Cynical America: The trouble with believing anything and nothing at the same time” Serwer brought attention to this interesting phenomenon. In this post, I give some examples of gullicism, make some comments about its causes, and opine about the danger that it poses in a world where the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) makes it increasingly difficult to know whether or not something is true.

Internet Trolls and Anti-Vaxxers

My first example of gullicism involves internet “trolls.” These are people who are very quick to call someone a liar and to forcefully spout an alternative explanation for which they have no evidence. An example involving myself occurred when I published an article explaining how I (author of a book about gullibility) was a victim of the Bernard Madoff Ponzi scheme. I was so offended by false claims saying that I made my Madoff victimhood up that I naively (and foolishly) provided my financial statements in an attempt to prove the truth of my claim. Being a relatively noncynical person, I chose to believe these were people of good will who could be helped to change their view if shown evidence. Now, sadly, I have become a little cynical myself about the motives and educability of trolls.

While trolling is typically not an organized event, gullibility comes in as trolls often influence each other. For example, when a University of California undergraduate recently went public about having been menaced by one of Berkeley’s many homeless people (who generally are completely harmless), she was accused by left-leaning trolls of having a conservative and racist political agenda. But trolls can be found at both ends of the political spectrum, as is true of gullicism generally.

The Anti-Vaxx movement can be considered a classic example of gullicism, with the cynicism part of a general opposition to conventional medical beliefs and the gullibility part of an organized belief—led by some outspoken health skeptics (such as RFK Jr.)—in alternative medical practices justified on the basis of ideology and faux evidence. In the political sphere, there are many examples of gullicism, one prominent example being widely believed cynical myths to the effect that former President Barack Obama lied about the country of his birth and also about many other things, such as having graduated from Columbia University.

The Four C's of Foolish Behavior

Using the factors in my “Four C’s” model of foolish behavior, I think I can explain the conspiracy theories that underlie these and other forms of gullicism. These four factors—cognition, conation, character, and context—usually work in combination, although individuals obviously vary in terms of the strength of the factors activated in a particular case. Briefly: (a) “cognition” comes into play as gullicists typically lack the ability to evaluate the evidence relating to certain beliefs; (b) “conation” comes into play as gullicists have emotional needs that cloud their judgment about what is truthful; (c) “character” comes into play as gullicists are high in both gullibility and cynicism personality traits; and (d) “context” comes into play when a situation has sufficient ambiguity and when a gullicist comes into contact with like-minded people.

I am writing these words at a time when there is much foment over the advent of AI and fear for its consequences for many spheres of life. I do not believe that the debate has touched specifically on gullicism, but it should. That is because AI’s blurring of the line between truth and falseness has the potential to do great harm, especially in the political sphere.

item.title: Why True Friends Are So Rare
item.description:
Friends

Why True Friends Are So Rare

Why the best friends tell us what we least want to hear.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility, pleasure, and virtue.
  • In the deepest friendships, we value people for who they are.
  • A true friend helps us become who we could be.
"Plato is dear, but dearer still is truth"—a saying that captures Aristotle’s willingness to disagree with his teacher in the pursuit of truth, and his conviction that genuine friendship need never fear honest disagreement.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Raphael/Public domain

What makes a true friend? Aristotle distinguishes friendships of utility, pleasure, and virtue—and explains why the finest friends are so rare.

Today, everyone is obsessed with romantic love. Aristotle, however, conceived of the highest human relationship in terms of friendship—the bond through which we learn to value another person for their own sake.

For the Greeks, true friendship was a rare and precious thing. In Plato’s Lysis, Socrates says, “I would rather have a real friend than all the gold of Darius [the Persian emperor], or even Darius himself.” But today, on social media, we call hundreds of people our friends.

By putting romantic love on a pedestal, we have devalued friendship. Our romantic partner is also expected to be our best friend, confidant, counsellor… As a result, other friendships may be neglected or even treated as threats.

Aristotle’s Three Kinds of Friendship

Friendship is so important to Aristotle’s account of the good life that he devotes two of the 10 books of the Nicomachean Ethics to it.

Aristotle famously distinguishes between three kinds of friendship: friendships of utility, friendships of pleasure, and friendships of virtue. In a friendship of utility, we value our friend for what they can bring us. In a friendship of pleasure, we value them for the enjoyment they provide. These relationships are not necessarily base: colleagues, neighbours, and tennis partners may genuinely like and help one another.

But the limitation of these first two kinds of friendship lies in their reason for being: When the advantage or pleasure fades, the friendship fades with it.

Why Perfect Friends Are so Rare

Lasting friendships, on the other hand, are based on character or virtue: Each friend values the other, not for what he brings, but for who he is. The friend’s well-being and flourishing become part of our own.

Because we are invested in the well-being and flourishing of our friend, we owe them the hard truth—and expect the same thing in return. A real friend does not simply accept us as we are but recognises our potential and helps us become what we could be.

That’s why “perfect friendship,” as Aristotle calls it, is not for everyone. Most people would sooner ghost us than listen to the truth about themselves—particularly now, when there are so many less demanding distractions around. Whereas social media affirms our public image, true friends challenge the person underneath.

You may also be interested in my companion piece, The True Meaning of Platonic Love.

item.title: Tired of Fixing Every Problem at Work?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Tired of Fixing Every Problem at Work?

Why high performers become exhausted by being indispensable.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • High achievers are often the default problem-solvers because they constantly deliver.
  • Routinely solving other people's problems can drain your own creativity.
  • Being needed becomes your identity, and stepping in feels automatic.
You can simultaneously be highly productive and creatively depleted.
Source: TheStandingDesk / Unsplash

People are afraid that artificial intelligence (AI) will take away their jobs, but there is a bigger urgency. Namely, the lack of time and inability to be creative and think deeply about a problem have taken away people’s desire to work. AI is not the problem. Being the person who fixes everything is an overlooked challenge that is disproportionately impacting high performers.

How many times have you sat in a meeting, watching the project go off course? One person is struggling with something you could resolve in an hour. The clock is ticking, the deadline is looming, and no one is stepping in to help.

How many times have you sat in an office meeting, seeing a problem spiral out of control, knowing that you could fix it? Or how about a program that needs rescuing? If you are like many of the high performers I’ve studied and coached, you probably think to yourself, “I can fix this, so I should.”

It makes sense. You are really good at solving problems, and can’t simply let things go, knowing you could fix it. The fixing has become reflexive. It’s also become your identity. You see the gap, inefficiency, mistake, or looming disaster before anyone else does, and you instinctively jump in. But should you?

When “I Can Fix It” Becomes “I Should Fix It”

Always volunteering to put out fires you never started has become what I call the Rescue Reflex. You naturally step in to solve a problem you know how to solve.

For high performers, the reflex is consistently reinforced because it always works. After doing it enough times, the problem-solving no longer feels deliberate. It becomes something natural. After all, if you see something broken or inefficient, how can you just leave it be?

So you fix the problem…again. The problem disappears, everyone is grateful, and it quickly becomes business as usual. It also becomes what you are relied on and therefore known for. You might get something out of it, too. There is a sense of satisfaction from being needed and useful. It is also exhausting. So there is a real conundrum.

You’ve now become the Office Mechanic, the person known for keeping everything running smoothly. You are always scanning for what needs fixing, a process that doesn’t give you a moment’s rest. You are always in a reactive mode. Even when you’ve averted one crisis, you are already noticing the next thing that needs fixing.

Productive, But Depleted

Before burnout appears, there are subtle clues that you are slowly disconnecting. You realize you’ve become invisible. You’re so busy executing that your previous sense of curiosity and wonder have dissipated, as have your interest and ability to do small experiments, deep thinking, and any desire to do something new. You’ve become a shell of your former self.

Not Every Problem Is Yours to Solve

Most people won’t notice it, as those activities are usually done behind closed doors. You are still executing and fixing, just no longer thinking. You can be highly productive and creatively depleted at the same time. If most of your mental bandwidth goes toward fixing what is constantly broken, there is less space to ask what could be reimagined and built.

The next time you see a problem you instinctively know how to solve, don’t reflexively say “How do I fix this?” Instead, ask “Does this need me?” Just because you could rescue something doesn’t mean it should be rescued by you.

item.title: While You Sleep, Your Brain Gets to Work
item.description:
Sleep

While You Sleep, Your Brain Gets to Work

Inside the remarkable sleep stages and what your brain is doing all night long.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Our brains are not inactive while we sleep.
  • Sleep is composed of four different sleep stages, each with unique brain wave patterns and health benefits.
  • Protecting seven to nine hours of sleep per night will help your brain cycle through all of the sleep stages.

Have you ever wondered what happens to your brain while you sleep? Could it be that your brain turns off just as the rest of your body shuts down for the night? For quite some time, scientists and physicians believed that to be the case. But this view changed with the invention of the electroencephalogram, or EEG, a device that records our brain’s electrical activity. In the 1920s and 1930s, when scientists first recorded the sleeping brain using EEG, they were shocked to discover that the brain was anything but quiet at night. Rather, the brain was considerably busy, cycling through distinct patterns of activity. Today, we know that sleep is anything but a passive process; instead, it’s composed of carefully orchestrated sleep stages, each with its own unique brain-wave patterns and health implications.

The sleeping brain in cycles

Typically, our sleep is composed of repeated sleep cycles that last between 90 and 120 minutes. Most of us cycle through four to six of these cycles per night. Physicians can watch this pattern in real time while a patient undergoes an overnight sleep study (polysomnogram), which records brain wave patterns, eye movements, heart activity, breathing patterns, and muscle tone.

With the advent of EEG monitoring, sleep was divided into two main categories: non-REM sleep/non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (further divided into three stages, N1, N2, and N3) and REM sleep (rapid eye movement). Most of us spend about three-quarters of the night in non-REM sleep, and the remaining time is spent in REM sleep.

When explaining to patients about the different sleep stages, I like to use the analogy of an ocean, where each sleep stage has you moving a little farther away from shore and deeper into the water.

  • Stage N1 sleep: Just stepping in. Stage N1 sleep is the transition between being awake and asleep. It’s considered the lightest stage of sleep, such that if you are woken up from N1 sleep, you could almost convince yourself that you weren’t sleeping at all. This would be a lot like walking from dry land into the shallowest part of the water. Your feet still feel the sand underneath, and the smallest thing can pull you right back onto the beach. This is also the briefest stage of sleep where most adults spend 2 to 5 percent of the night.
  • Stage N2 sleep: Wading deeper into the water. Stage N2 sleep comprises the largest share of our sleep, anywhere from 45 to 55 percent of the night. Using our ocean analogy, this stage is as though you’ve walked a bit farther into the water, but you could still turn around and walk easily back to shore. You’re also more relaxed in the water. This is the stage where your heart rate and body temperature drop, your breathing steadies, and muscles relax. In stage N2 sleep, your body is preparing to enter the deepest stage of sleep. What role does this stage play in our overall health? It’s the stage responsible for consolidating memory and learning, whereby the brain is filing away things you learned and practiced during the day.
  • Stage N3 sleep/deep sleep: Floating in calm, deep water. Stage N3 sleep, also known as deep sleep, is the deepest stage of sleep. It’s also called slow-wave sleep because of the types of brain waves captured on EEG recordings. Overall, we spend about 10 to 20 percent of the night in stage N3 sleep. This is the sleep stage that is hardest to wake from. If you are woken up from deep sleep, you often feel groggy and disoriented for a few minutes. You can think of this stage as you floating in calm but deep water with a body that is fully relaxed. The goal of this stage is brain recovery. Research has shown that deep sleep helps the brain with a type of cleanup after a busy day. Individuals with reduced or impaired stage 3 sleep may be at risk for Alzheimer's dementia.
  • REM (rapid eye movement): The rushing water around you. REM sleep is where the brain shifts from being relaxed to heightened activity. In fact, the brain wave patterns associated with REM sleep resemble being awake. Our eyes dart back and forth under our eyelids (hence the “rapid eye movement” name), and our heart rate and breathing speed up. Thankfully, our muscles are temporarily paralyzed; otherwise, we would run the risk of physically acting out our dreams. Returning to our ocean analogy, REM sleep is when the water comes alive and starts rushing and moving all around you. This is also the stage where we do most of our dreaming. What’s the purpose of REM sleep? REM is thought to play a key role in emotional processing, where our brains process our feelings and file away certain memories. We spend about 20 to 25 percent of the night in this sleep stage.

What does this mean for you tonight?

The most important message I want you to understand is that while you can’t consciously control any individual sleep stage, you can set yourself up for success by protecting conditions that let the entire sleep sequence run undisturbed.

The following three habits will help protect all four sleep stages, ensuring you get the benefit from each:

  1. Get enough sleep by targeting seven to nine hours of sleep per night. A full night of sleep will give your brain and body time to cycle through all the sleep stages. This is important as we get most of our deep sleep in the first half of the night while REM sleep happens in the early morning hours.
  2. Keep a consistent sleep schedule. A fixed bedtime and wake time every night is the strongest factor helping you get consolidated sleep.
  3. Make your bedroom dark, cool, and quiet. A cool bedroom (60-70°F/16-19°C) that’s also dark and quiet can protect you from disturbances that would otherwise disrupt your sleep.

While scientists thought the brain was inactive while we slept, we now know that this couldn’t be further from the truth. When we sleep, our brain choreographs an intricate dance of brain processes in different sleep stages, each of which plays an important role in our overall health. Help your brain get the benefit of all these stages by protecting and prioritizing your sleep—starting tonight.

item.title: Why a Healthy Mind Is Inseparably Linked to Life
item.description:
Environment

Why a Healthy Mind Is Inseparably Linked to Life

Can we solve the massive mental health crisis we face, and if so, how?

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Consciousness is the direct expression of the quality of our living nature.
  • A healthy mind, which is rooted in one's quality of life, makes life worth living.
  • Solving our mental health crisis starts with the enrichment of life.
Every natural mind is an expression of life
Source: Mi Pham/Unsplash

This is the first post in a series about our quest for a fulfilling life. We begin by delving into the roots of experience. To do so, we will draw on some key insights from Richard Davidson and Antonio Damasio.

Why are we experiencing a massive mental health crisis? According to Richard Davidson, the founder and director of the Center for Healthy Minds at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, depression is now the leading cause of morbidity globally. Suicide rates are increasing and distractibility and concentration impairments are at an all-time high (Davidson & Dahl, 2026, p. 5).

We suffer when we see the world news. William James's search for what makes life worth living is more relevant than ever. Soon, we will have to share the planet with almost 10 billion people. How will we manage? I believe that understanding the nature of experience is a good place to start.

The Living Origin of Our Consciousness

Damasio’s research shows that consciousness arises from “feelings of existence”: quiet, continuous sensations of the body as it experiences itself while constantly regulating itself. These sensations form the living basis of consciousness.

From this living foundation arises an organism’s ability to know that it exists. And from that knowledge, the mind emerges. The mind is a living dynamic. It is the form that life takes when it perceives itself.

The Play of Consciousness

Antonio Damasio touches on the core of consciousness in a sentence from his new book:

"In this play that is consciousness, the mind, so noble, and the body, so modest, are forever united" (Damasio, 2026, p. 145).

This simple sentence touches on the nature of consciousness. Its implications are revolutionary. Here, Damasio is not arguing that the body and mind are two separate phenomena that work together or influence each other. Rather, he is suggesting something much more radical: that consciousness exists only as a unity of body and mind. There is no mind without life. There is no identity without embodied sensitivity. Mental health cannot be considered separately from the quality of this interplay between life and the mental.

This proposition lies at the heart of a psychology that begins with life rather than cognition.

What This Means for the Enrichment of Consciousness

Does a healthy mind make life worth living? If so, then mental health — as an enrichment of our consciousness — is deeply rooted in the quality of our environment, the rhythms of our lives, the sensitivity of our relationships, the permeability of our bodies and the ecological integrity of our existence. This immediately highlights the threats to our mental health.

In other words, mental health is an ecological issue.

Burnout is not an individual failure, but rather a mismatch between our living spirit and our cultural rhythms.

Depression is a loss of meaning in this world.

Anxiety signals disconnection between our lives and the world.

When our spirit is alive, it suffers when life becomes impoverished.

An Uncomfortable Truth

Many modern views of the mind are based on the implicit assumption that the mind is separate from life. We talk about 'mental processes', 'executive functions' and 'information processing', as if the mind were a kind of software that is separate from the body. This idea is appealing because it suggests that we can control our minds. However, empirically, it is untenable.

Damasio’s research highlights this. It confronts us with the uncomfortable truth that all views of the mind that are separate from life are scientifically unfounded. This requires a cultural shift that is by no means obvious. After all, it means we must reconsider our psychology and the cultural assumptions that accompany it.

The uncomfortable truth is that our actions are not always aligned with our identity. We are not beings who exist outside of life. Any notion of a supernatural world is probably just a cultural construct.

Take the facts we could see and experience every day last summer, for example: the heat-related deaths, the massive wildfires, the drought and the incessant drones dropping bombs on innocent families. This is a culture at odds with who we are.

Enriching Psychology

The mind is alive. Identity emerges when the body becomes self-aware and engages with the living world and its relationships. A healthy mind is not a mental construct, but a living configuration of sensitivity. It arises from permeability. It arises from resonance. It arises from the capacity to be moved.

Damasio has uncovered its biological roots. My recent work explores its psychological, relational and cultural implications. Together, these contributions form a single movement: a return to a living mind that enriches our consciousness and makes life worth living again.

Why This Is Necessary Now

Our culture is at a turning point. We are living in an era of mental overload, fragmented identities and ecological alienation. Our spirits have become disconnected from their origins. Psychology that reconnects the spirit with life is not a luxury — it is a necessity.

When the spirit is alive, care becomes second nature. When the spirit is alive, resonance becomes possible again. Identity becomes a relationship rather than a construct. Culture once again becomes a living environment for humanity.

Conclusion

Damasio’s statement is not just poetic embellishment. Rather, it is an empirical assertion that reconnects psychology with life itself. The mind is alive, and this changes everything.

Hope arises when we connect the lifelong insights of the two important psychologists Antonio Damasio and Richard Davidson. Enriching our consciousness with a healthy mind that is deeply rooted in life may be the first step towards resolving the significant mental health crisis we are currently facing.

Consciousness is not a phenomenon that transcends nature. Rather, it is the spontaneous expression of our living nature. We are not who we think we are. We are who we experience we are. We are the beings that have evolved on this planet for billions of years.

Culture must acknowledge its teacher here. A healthy mind rooted in quality of life enriches consciousness, making life worth living. So yes, we can resolve the deep mental health crisis if we start by recognizing that consciousness and nature are interconnected.

item.title: The 'Mentally Ill Addict'
item.description:
Addiction

The 'Mentally Ill Addict'

Why addiction is a mental illness and what that means.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Someone's continued substance use or risky behavior after it causes suffering can feel baffling.
  • Addiction changes brain structure, specifically in areas controlling reward, stress, and self-control.
  • Psychology classifies addiction as a mental illness; understanding this reduces shame and promotes treatment.

If someone continues to use a drug or keeps engaging in some kind of risky behavior after losing relationships, health, and/or employment, or getting in legal trouble, it can feel baffling. We wonder: If it’s causing pain and suffering in their life, why don't they simply stop doing it? Many people will look at the situation and think the person really ought to make more of an effort—that addiction reflects a person’s weak character or that they simply aren’t adept at making good choices.

Source: Samantha Stein

But modern psychology and neuroscience understand addiction differently and have come to classify it as a mental disorder. This is because brain imaging shows that, over time, addiction actually changes brain structure and function, specifically in areas controlling reward, stress, and self-control. In other words, changes in the brain and body turn voluntary drug use or risky behaviors into a chronic, compulsive brain disease. These brain changes affect motivation, reward, learning, self-control, and behavior, which is why the person’s behavior persists despite serious consequences. Science, in other words, has fundamentally changed how we understand addiction, and why we now call it a mental illness.

What Is Mental Illness?

It might be helpful to back up and explain how we classify something as a mental illness. The American Psychological Association defines a mental illness as an impairment or disturbance in thoughts, feelings, or behaviors that causes distress and/or impairment. Prolonged substance abuse and repetitive engagement in destructive or risky behaviors meet these criteria because the person has lost control over their behavior, it impairs their thinking and emotions, and they are continuing to use or engage in the behavior despite the harm it’s causing them and others.

Addiction as Mental Illness

Addiction is officially understood as a chronic mental disease of brain reward, motivation, memory, and related circuitry. It affects dopamine learning and executive functioning, contains cravings, and is habit-forming. An individual with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) might repeatedly lock and unlock doors to regulate their anxiety and stop the intrusive thoughts, even if they know rationally that action isn’t actually going to keep them any safer. A person suffering from depression might repeatedly crawl into bed even if they have read the research on the importance of exercise in combating depression. When our brain is malfunctioning, we are sometimes powerless to stop or start an action that isn’t rational. This is where it’s helpful to understand it as a disorder: Similar to the person with OCD or depression, when someone is in addiction, their brain isn’t able to think rationally. Their decision-making is impaired. When they try to halt the substance use or behavior, it creates distress, and, thus, their brain has become rewired—their behavior has become compulsive rather than based on a decision.

This is why, while many people may say, "This person suffers from addiction and mental illness," treatment providers will say, "This person is suffering from two mental illnesses." Addiction is one of them.

Why Does It Matter?

Why does calling addiction a mental illness matter? For several reasons. First, it reduces moral blame—not only is it inaccurate to call addiction a weakness, but it’s also entirely unhelpful. Second, it encourages treatment—people are more likely to seek the help they need if they understand how difficult it can be to “just stop.” Additionally, understanding it as a mental illness can improve public policy and therefore access to needed treatment. Finally, it recognizes that addiction is, in fact, treatable. It’s an illness that can be helped.

Understanding It as a Mental Illness Is Not the End of the Story

All of that said, it’s important we understand that just because addiction is a mental illness, it doesn’t mean people should not be held accountable for their behavior. Brain changes help explain behaviors, but they don’t excuse them or remove responsibility. Understanding biology improves treatment, but recovery still requires a decision for someone to make that they need to make a change and hard work to make it happen. The question is not “Why won’t they stop?” It’s “Why is stopping so difficult—and how can intervention and treatment help rewire the brain so different choices can be made?”

item.title: The Hybrid Scarcity of Values
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Hybrid Scarcity of Values

What our salaries, status, and security reveal about what we (really) value.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Humans are highly responsive to visible signals of status.
  • Care, trust, friendship, community contribution, and stewardship are harder to count.
  • The abundance of things produced by generative technology may tempt us to consume more and appreciate less.
If AI abundance pushes us see the difference between visible and valuable, it might help us correct a major gap of modern life: confusing what is expensive with what is precious.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

Consider two humans beginning work at 8 in the morning. One enters an air-conditioned office, opens a laptop, and spends the day moving information: numbers, contracts, forecasts, emails, and presentations. The other helps an elderly person out of bed, changes sheets, prepares food, cleans a bathroom, administers reassurance, and notices whether a small change in expression signals pain, confusion, or fear. Both jobs can require skill, discipline, and responsibility. Yet, in many economies, the first is far more likely to come with higher pay, greater status, predictable hours, better social protection, and a comfortable retirement plan.

That difference does not prove that office work is overvalued, nor that difficult physical work should automatically command the highest salary. Wages emerge from productivity, scarcity, bargaining power, credentials, ownership, institutions, and proximity to revenue. The problem starts when we allow that market price to become our moral price list. A salary is a number, and numbers acquire authority. Over time, what the market pays can begin to feel like a ranking of what society values; vice versa, social values shape the price tag of human time and effort. The resulting hierarchy sits uneasily beside the conditions human beings actually need to flourish.

The pay-slip as a value signal

The contradiction is especially clear in work societies cannot function without. The International Labour Organization's global study of essential work found that key employees—including workers in food systems, cleaning, transport, security, and health—earned on average 26 percent less than other employees, while one in three was low-paid. These workers were also more exposed to temporary contracts, irregular hours, physical and biological hazards, and limited access to training or social protection. The COVID-19 pandemic briefly made their contribution impossible to miss. Societies applauded nurses, cleaners, delivery workers, and supermarket staff because ordinary life had suddenly revealed how dependent it was on them. The applause faded faster than the underlying pay structures changed.

Care work makes the paradox even harder to ignore. Population aging is increasing demand, yet the OECD's Health at a Glance 2025 describes long-term care as struggling to attract and retain workers because of low wages, high physical and mental risks, nonstandard contracts, and low recognition. More than one in three long-term-care workers across reporting OECD countries worked part-time, and around one in six held fixed-term contracts. These are not peripheral jobs. They sit at the point where aging, dignity, health, and family life meet. Yet the material conditions attached to them often communicate that the work is replaceable and the worker expendable. (And yet—can't the same be said about any work and the person who performs it?)

The care paradox

A 2025 ILO working paper on the valuation of women's work makes the mismatch uncomfortably concrete. Drawing on decades of U.S. labor-market data, the researchers found that social skills carry significant wage premiums in business services, while comparable skills receive no similar reward in care occupations, where compassion, communication, patience, and interpersonal judgment are central to the job. We seem comfortable paying for relationship skills when they help manage clients, deals, and organizations, then discounting many of the same capacities when they are directed toward children, older people, or those who are ill. This type of value discrimination is a question of mindsets, not facts.

This tells us something about value systems as much as labor markets. Ask people what matters most, and the answers are remarkably stable: health, family, friendship, dignity, security, purpose, kindness. Now inspect the architecture of everyday life. Which occupations receive the largest salaries?

Flourishing has more than one currency

Our economic instincts are reinforced by psychology. Humans are highly responsive to visible signals of status, and salary, title, office size, and professional prestige give us convenient shorthand for importance. Care, trust, friendship, community contribution, and stewardship are harder to count. What can be measured and monetized therefore tends to dominate attention. Yet the science of well-being points in a wider direction. The Global Flourishing Study, involving more than 200,000 participants across 22 countries, treats flourishing as multidimensional: Happiness and life satisfaction sit alongside physical and mental health, meaning and purpose, character and virtue, close relationships and financial security. Its 2026 longitudinal work is extending that picture across time, examining how balance among areas of life relates to dozens of later well-being outcomes. The underlying lesson is straightforward: A good life has several currencies, and income is only one of them.

Artificial intelligence (AI) makes this discrepancy more visible because many forms of information work are becoming easier to reproduce. Standard summaries, routine reports, presentations, basic images, and first-pass analysis can now be generated at negligible marginal cost. Much embodied and relational work remains stubbornly resistant to such scaling.

From stated values to visible values

A useful way to test that choice is to examine four receipts of value.

  • The first is money: Where does compensation flow, and does it bear any relationship to responsibility, difficulty, risk, and social contribution?
  • The second is time: What activities and relationships receive protected hours rather than whatever remains after work expands to fill the week?
  • The third is status: Whose expertise receives visibility, voice, and respect?
  • The fourth is security: Who receives stable contracts, health care, training, parental leave, and retirement protection? These four signals are imperfect, yet together they reveal far more about priorities than mission statements, speeches, or annual values campaigns.

The same audit works personally. Look at your spending over the previous month (instead of the principles you endorse when asked about). Where did your money go? What received your best hours rather than your leftovers? Whom did you thank, praise, or promote? What did you protect when the calendar became crowded? The answers form a surprisingly accurate values statement. Appreciation becomes credible when it changes allocation.

Generative technology may give us an abundance of things that once appeared scarce. That abundance could tempt us to produce and consume even more and appreciate that abundance even less. At the same time, this moment also offers an opportunity to reconsider the value of scarcity itself. If the age of artificial abundance can help us see beyond the visible layers of abundance, it may also help us correct one of the oldest errors in modern life: confusing what is expensive with what is precious.

item.title: Including a Partner in Erectile Difficulty Treatment
item.description:
Sex

Including a Partner in Erectile Difficulty Treatment

Erectile difficulty involves more than just the person experiencing it.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Couples who go through treatment together report better sexual and relationship outcomes.
  • Open communication of desires and boundaries can dispel the assumptions that happen in silence.
  • Even a single joint session can help couples understand how to better support one another.

Most men who seek treatment for erectile difficulty often do it alone. They research solutions online, order prescriptions through an app, or visit a health provider all on their own. Sometimes they do so without ever telling a partner what they are worried about or how they are trying to resolve it.

That’s understandable. Erectile issues can challenge a man’s sense of himself—his masculinity, his age, his health, his worth. Embarrassment and shame try to protect us from those vulnerabilities by saying, “Keep it to yourself. No one will understand. You have to solve this on your own.”

The reality is that erectile problems frequently occur in the context of relationships, whether that’s short-term encounters or long-term partnerships. There is certainly benefit in starting with individual work, learning how to navigate anxiety or a changing body. It is also invaluable to include a partner when one is present.

While I focus on the relational context in this post, please note there are many cases when erectile troubles occur on one’s own or when single. You don’t have to be partnered to feel distressed or to seek help.

What Gets Missed in Individual Treatment

Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

A partner’s experience is important for many reasons. They might be suffering in their own way, they may be unintentionally contributing to the problem, and/or the man may be making assumptions about the partner’s experience. Most importantly, including a partner can improve treatment outcomes.

The following case is a composite with client details anonymized to protect privacy.

Devon did not want to involve his partner Priya in a joint session. She often cried when they talked about his erection difficulty, and he feared involving her in treatment would make the problem feel even bigger. He knew she was expecting intercourse and was disappointed he couldn’t maintain his erections. He wanted to solve the problem before involving her.

As it turned out later, his assumptions about her experience were a little off the mark.

Partners commonly interpret a man’s erectile difficulty as evidence about themselves—that they are unattractive or undesirable, or that the man has lost interest in them. When this fear heightens, they may doubt the man’s fidelity or his sexuality.

Without accurate information, those interpretations don’t get corrected. The partner doesn’t know what to do. Should they try initiating more contact? Less? The stress becomes bottled and pressurized until it feels like there’s no way to talk about the problem.

Devon no longer pursued Priya like he did when they were dating. She worried his erection problems were further proof that he was no longer attracted to her. She wanted him to initiate contact, which helped her feel desired. She couldn’t ask for that without feeling like she was burdening him, forcing him into intimacy that he didn’t really want.

Both Devon and Priya misinterpreted each other’s behavior and had difficulty communicating their concerns openly, fearing the other’s judgment. Until they were both present in therapy, Devon didn’t know that Priya’s expectations of sex were actually quite broad, and Priya didn’t have insight into the pressure Devon was feeling. That changed once they started talking.

What This Looks Like in Practice

There are many options for including a partner in therapy. The right approach depends on the couple.

A single joint session can sometimes be enough to get everyone on the same page—to clarify any errors in assumptions and lower expectations. Other times, it’s useful to have a recurring joint session every few weeks or months to check in on progress and identify new challenges, recurring barriers, and opportunities for support.

For some couples, it can be beneficial to start couples therapy. Ongoing sessions can be particularly useful when the relationship’s troubles go beyond the sexual realm, when their goals are misaligned, when communication skills could be strengthened, or when sexual problems persist over time.

Research has shown that when a man is treated for erectile difficulty, sexual function and satisfaction tend to improve for both the man and his partner, even if the partner is not actively included in the treatment. That said, these positive outcomes are more likely when the client and his partner both want to be involved.

Adherence to a treatment plan is also stronger when a partner is involved. A joint session creates the opportunity to make decisions together—like whether to try medication or to change what sex looks like for a while.

Partnered therapy isn’t always possible. Some men are single, dating casually, or in relationships where a partner isn’t willing or able to participate. In those cases, there can still be benefit in processing how a client interacts with current or future partners: how they disclose their erectile difficulty, how they state their desires and boundaries, and how they check in with a partner’s experience.

Devon ultimately agreed to a joint session with Priya. He initially panicked when she started to cry in session. However, he was able to hear that her tears were not coming from disappointment about his performance but fear and doubt about her own self-worth. Their physical distance ended in that moment when he extended a hand to comfort her. She met his eyes, relieved that he initiated closeness.

Once Devon knew that Priya’s sexual satisfaction didn’t depend solely on his erections, he felt greater freedom to be intimate. He also became more open about his experience. When erectile difficulty was just an accepted fact of their sex life, they both felt less shame. It was no longer a weighty subject.

Devon’s openness in turn helped Priya feel reassured, knowing he was concerned about their sex life and actively trying to improve it. She realized her silence was creating space for Devon to fear the worst and made an effort to be more direct and specific with her own desires. She also learned that his erections weren’t the sole proof of his attraction to her.

After a few sessions together, they left with a shared plan for the future instead of working on two separate strategies in the dark.
