item.title: Building Team Cultures That Support Mental Health
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Building Team Cultures That Support Mental Health

Kevin Love Fund and NAMI help teen athletes ask for help and support teammates.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • The Kevin Love Fund and NAMI created a free lesson to help teen athletes talk about mental health.
  • Athletes can learn that asking for help is a sign of strength.
  • Coaches and teammates can help create cultures where athletes feel safe speaking up.

This month, I caught back up with the Kevin Love Fund (KLF), founded by NBA champion and mental health advocate Kevin Love, to discuss its new collaboration with the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI).

The two organizations recently launched Real Talk: Strength in Seeking Support, a free lesson designed to help teen athletes discuss emotional challenges, recognize when they or a teammate may need support, and feel more comfortable asking for help.

The goal of the program is to build team cultures that promote openness around mental health by:

  • Helping teen athletes build mental health awareness,
  • Strengthening emotional skills, and
  • Creating more supportive team environments.

NAMI CEO Daniel Gillison and KLF director of education Ellie Foster, who developed the lesson with NAMI advisors, took a moment to share their thoughts on the new program.

Source: Courtesy of KLF

Inside the Program

Foster took me inside the lesson, which incorporates research-backed strategies and expert guidance for destigmatizing conversations about mental health between teammates and coaches.

Foster emphasized the importance of normalizing conversations about mental health through short videos of athletes sharing stories of resilience, which can inspire others and help teens feel less alone. Drawing on research demonstrating the role of educator vulnerability in normalizing emotional discussions on athletic teams, the lesson encourages coaches to model similar openness (Foster, 2023).

The lesson also engages athletes in hands-on activities that allow them to practice expressing their emotions through creative outlets (e.g., writing, creating playlists), which is supported by research on arts-based approaches to supporting mental health (Stuckey & Nobel, 2010).

Ultimately, the lesson encourages athletes to see caring for their mental health and supporting one another as essential parts of being a teammate through asking the following questions:

  • How am I really doing?
  • What might I notice if a teammate is struggling?
  • How can I check in with someone?
  • And what can I do if I, myself, need support?
NAMI CEO Daniel H. Gillison, Jr.
Source: Courtsey of NAMI

Redefining Strength

Gillison is a former student-athlete himself and wishes he had learned earlier that being strong and asking for help are not opposites.

“Sometimes strength is recognizing when you need help and being willing to ask for it,” he said.

Sport teaches athletes to push through discomfort and not let the team down. But those lessons, when left unchecked, can be harmful.

According to Gillison, the problem comes when athletes see “pushing through” as the only way forward. Showing strength as an athlete can also look like:

  • Knowing your limits,
  • Recognizing when something isn’t right, and
  • Having the courage to ask for help.

He also shared his hope that teen athletes understand that being strong is not just about how they perform, but also about:

  • Taking care of yourself,
  • Looking out for the people around you, and
  • Knowing that none of us has to go through the hard things alone.

Supporting Teammates

I asked Gillison what a teen athlete should do when they recognize that a teammate may be struggling but worry about overreacting or betraying their trust.

He emphasized that teen athletes do not need to have all the answers or know exactly what to say to help a teammate. “Sometimes just showing up can make all the difference,” Daniel shared alongside the following guidance:

  • Start by checking in;
  • Let your teammate know you’ve noticed something seems different and that you’re there to listen; and
  • If you’re concerned about their safety or well-being, reach out to a trusted adult.

Gillison emphasized that this is not about betraying a teammate’s trust, but about looking out for them:

“Being a good friend and a good teammate sometimes means caring enough to speak up when something doesn’t seem right.”

Creating Cultures of Well-Being

We can tell athletes it is OK to ask for help, but the environment has to be safe enough to receive that request.

Gillison shared that, while we put a lot of responsibility on teen athletes to speak up when they are struggling, they will not do so unless they believe that someone will listen and support them in return.

This starts with coaches, parents, and teammates creating an environment where mental health is part of the conversation, not something that only comes up when there’s a crisis. Daniel recommends the following actions:

  • Check in,
  • Listen without judgment,
  • Know where to turn for help, and
  • Make sure athletes know that speaking up isn’t going to cost them playing time or change how people see them.

In fact, NAMI’s work with student-athletes has revealed that teens want their parents and coaches to reach out to them with mental health information and resources.

Foster shared that this is one reason the partnership with NAMI is so powerful; it allows athletes to connect with a trusted resource for additional mental health support when they need it, such as NAMI's Teen & Young Adult Helpline and local resources. Coaches and educators play a crucial role in helping athletes learn about the resources available to them.

“Our lesson with NAMI is designed to begin the conversation about mental health, and we believe that it will contribute to creating a team culture where relying on all of the support in the school and community becomes a normal part of what it means to be an athlete,” said Foster.

Source: Courtesy of KLF

The Foundation Is the Same

Storytelling has been central to Love’s advocacy. Foster shared that KLF continues to prioritize creating space for athletes to share their stories of challenge and resilience as a central part of building an athletic culture that supports athlete mental health.

“Most importantly, the lesson underscores that vulnerability is a choice—one athletes can make intentionally, when they are ready,” says Foster.

It was only fitting, then, that I ask Love himself why this partnership means so much to him.

“For a long time, I thought being a good teammate meant keeping whatever I was going through to myself. I worried that if people knew I was struggling, they would see me differently,” he replied.

Love believes that teen athletes today are carrying many of the same fears he did. The lesson aims to give these athletes the words to say they are having a hard time, while also helping the people around them know how to respond.

One of the most powerful aspects of the lesson is that it meets teen athletes where they are and leverages influential people in their own environment (e.g., coaches, educators, athletic communities) to establish cultures where mental health is treated as an essential part of overall well-being and performance.

“I wish I’d understood earlier that you can love your sport, be committed to your team, and still need help. You don’t have to earn that support by playing well.” –Kevin Love

item.title: Need a Boost? Nature Supports Better Well-Being
item.description:
Environment

Need a Boost? Nature Supports Better Well-Being

Natural environments can provide healing, restore focus, and improve well-being.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Hundreds of studies support the value of being in nature in a variety of domains.
  • There are several psychological theories behind why natural spaces are essential for our minds and bodies.
  • Deliberate, mindful engagement with nature is the most effective way to practice 'nature noticing.'

Humans have valued nature's importance for health and well-being for centuries in a variety of ancient traditions, but empirical research supporting its psychological and physiological benefits has only emerged in recent decades.

While we know that the natural world offers us opportunities for beautiful scenery and possible vacation destinations, the notion of nature as scientifically proven to be healing and restorative is less well known.

Source: Sandra Wartski

Room with a View

The landmark study demonstrating the connection between exposure to nature and health recovery was led by Dr. Roger Ulrich in 1984.1 He found that patients in a hospital recovering from surgery did better if they had a window overlooking green space. The patients whose window faced a brick wall used more pain medication, had longer hospital stays, and had more negative interactions with nurses during the recovery process. This was an amazing discovery.

Around that same time in the early 1980s, the concept of Forest Bathing (“shinrin-yoku”) was being introduced in Japan; however, the scientific research to support its benefits did not emerge until the early 2000’s2. The studies exploring the benefits of being in nature have continued to be varied, interesting, and expansive – and all continue to support the power of nature.

Source: Sandra Wartski

A Flood of Findings

Since the early 1980s, hundreds of studies have been conducted around the world, and they continue to support the basic conclusion that nature is good for us. Some of the research is correlational (observing patterns between variables that naturally exist), while other research is experimental (variables are controlled, allowing more conclusions about cause-and-effect). There are pros and cons to both approaches, but the results continue to show the value of spending time outdoors for our mental and physical health.

Creativity and ingenuity abound in the nature research, with scientists utilizing a variety of measures, from surveys to spit, blood to behaviors, heart rate monitors to headsets (such as a mobile Electroencephalography or EEG headset to measure brainwave activity). Results consistently support the natural world as providing opportunities for regeneration, resilience, renewal, and repair3.

Source: Sandra Wartski

Many Downstream Benefits

As the research on the benefits of connecting with nature expands, it becomes increasingly difficult to adequately capture all of the advantages; however, offered here are three examples in the domains of physical, psychological, and cognitive.

The impact of nature on physical health was one of the earliest domains to be studied. Physical health benefits often include decreased blood pressure, lower heart rate, reduced adrenaline, increased parasympathetic/relaxation system activation, and improved immune function. Dr. Qing Li led one study highlighting this benefit4. His team tracked healthy adults during a 3-day, 2-night trip to a Japanese forest. They collected blood and urine samples before, during, and after the trip to investigate molecular and immunological changes that occur in the human body during forest immersion. They found a 50% surge in immune protection, along with a spike in an anti-cancer protein. Just as amazing was the finding that the enhanced immune boost lasted for more than 30 days after returning to city life.

The benefits of nature on psychological health include increased mood, decreased anxiety, lower stress, and higher joy. A research example that masterfully highlighted the joy factor was led by Drs. MacKerron & Mourato,5 who had 20,000 subjects utilize the Mappiness Smartphone App, which randomly pinged them throughout the day to ask several questions and track their exact GPS coordinates. Findings showed that subjects were significantly happier when they were outdoors in any natural area. This “happiness boost” was significant even after controlling for what the person was doing, who they were with, current weather, and time of day.

The research on nature positively impacting cognitive functioning includes findings of improved performance, increased creativity, enhanced performance speed, and better attentional abilities. One research example by Dr. Lee6 and colleagues studied 150 students who were asked to engage in a dull, attention-draining computer task. Halfway through, participants were given a brief 40-second break; half of the group was asked to look at a digital image of a bare concrete city rooftop while the other half was asked to look at a digital image of a city rooftop covered in a flowering meadow. The group that looked at the flowering nature scene made significantly fewer mistakes and were found to show much more consistent alertness for the second half of the task.

Source: Michael Podger/Unsplash

There Is a Web of Multifaceted Causal Theories

The specific mechanism of how nature helps in such a powerful way is still unclear, but there are several hypotheses of what is at the root of the benefits7, including the positive impact of multisensory input, smells (such as phytoncides), sights (such as fractals), good bacteria in the soil, reconnection to our biophilic ancestors, or the tendency to engage in more movement in nature.

There are two primary foundational causal theories: ART and SRT. Attention Restoration Theory (ART)8 posits that spending time in nature replenishes cognitive resources depleted by sustained mental focus and that soft, effortless focus assists in the attention fatigue of our modern environments. Stress Reduction Theory (SRT)9 proposes that humans experience positive affective responses and parasympathetic nervous system activation during most types of nature contact. As with so many theories offered in science, there is assumed overlap and bidirectional influence on all of these benefits.

Source: Sandra Wartski

The Nature Prescription

Being in nature and getting more “Vitamin N” (coined by Richard Louv10) is invaluable for our self-care and healthcare. Finding ways to connect to the natural world is especially important given our increasingly urban, indoors, digital-focused population in the modern age, with current estimates suggesting that over 90% of Americans spend their time indoors and children spend 50% less time outdoors than previous generations11.

When approaching nature, it is recommended that individuals seek out local settings while pursuing variation whenever possible. Being mindfully focused on the senses is recommended as a means of being more fully present. A hurried dash to one’s car doesn’t quite count, nor does a cell phone-focused shuffle to the mailbox. Going big and going small are also recommended as a means of looking for the large, vast, and awe-inspiring (a tall tree, waterfall, mountains) as well as the beautiful complexities of the micro-vast (an ant hill, a blooming flower, moss on a stone). Major movement is not required; presence and noticing are.

And even if getting outside is not possible for certain people or on certain days, the benefits of vicarious or indirect exposure to nature are well established. Looking out the window at nature, watching nature shows, playing bird songs, or having a potted plant inside have been found to have psychological and physiological benefits as well12.

Source: Mark Wartski/Used with permission

Recommended amounts of time in nature vary, but research suggests that spending at least 120 minutes per week in nature is associated with better health and well-being13. This can be spread across the week in small increments or done all at once when time allows.

In summary: get out.

item.title: ADHD Isn’t a Disorder or a Myth. It’s a Mismatch.
item.description:
ADHD

ADHD Isn’t a Disorder or a Myth. It’s a Mismatch.

Moving beyong a false dichotomy.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • The standard view holds that ADHD is a brain disorder rooted in faulty “executive functioning.”
  • A growing body of research suggests ADHD may instead be a cognitive style mismatched to modern classrooms.
  • Reframing ADHD as a mismatch, not a disorder or myth, changes who bears responsibility for fixing the problem.

One in 10 American kids is diagnosed with ADHD. About half of them are on stimulant medication, such as amphetamine-based drugs like Adderall. That's about 3 million kids.

These kids are all given the same story. They have a brain disorder called “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.” It stems from a defect in something called “executive functioning” — a hypothetical brain system. This defect can be corrected by medication.

There are mental health professionals who criticize the dominant narrative. However, they often err on the opposite side by suggesting that ADHD is no more than a “myth,” as suggested by a new UK documentary, The Great ADHD Myth?

Source: cottonbro studio/Pexels

The film claims that there’s a spectrum of normal variation in kids with respect to distractibility and inattention. Doctors have drawn an arbitrary line near the lower end of the spectrum – but otherwise, ADHD has no biological reality.

Yet there’s an emerging insight in ADHD research — arrived at by numerous investigators in different fields, including neuroscience, anthropology, and psychology. The ADHD mind is neither a defect nor a myth. It's a unique cognitive style, mismatched to an environment it was never built for.

ADHD as an Evolutionary Mismatch

The emerging theory is that ADHD is likely a distinct cognitive style with its own strengths, one that was designed for certain kinds of environments.

Think about the needs of a nomadic community. It needs explorers — people who will discover new water sources, new sources of food, new ways of watching for large predators. Once something is found, the community needs exploiters — people who make efficient, sustained use of what's been discovered.

The psychologist Helen Taylor calls this “complementary cognition”: a division of cognitive labor between explorers and exploiters.

People with ADHD traits would naturally have made the best explorers. Novelty-seeking, hands-on learning, and drifting attention would have been exactly the traits needed to make those crucial discoveries.

Now suppose you take somebody with this distinctive cognitive style and place them in a modern classroom, forced to sit for hours at a time listening to someone talk. Something has gone terribly wrong — but not in the kid's mind. What's gone wrong is the mismatch between the person and the environment they've been placed in.

The Science Behind the Mismatch

Incidentally, the idea of an evolutionary mismatch isn't some evolutionary “just-so” story. It's based on a flood of actual research.

For example, a little over a decade ago, anthropologist Dan Eisenberg and colleagues studied the Ariaal, a population in northern Kenya that includes both traditionally nomadic pastoralists and a settled minority who've shifted to agriculture and the market economy.

Among the settled Ariaal, people with ADHD-linked traits were less well-nourished than their peers, as measured by body mass index. Among the nomadic Ariaal, the opposite was true: those with the same traits were healthier and better-fed.

The exact same cognitive skills that let them thrive in a nomadic community caused them to suffer in a sedentary one.

Along these lines, evolutionary biologists have even gathered evidence that ADHD traits might’ve supported global migration during the Last Ice Age.

Research in cognitive science supports the same idea of mismatch, not dysfunction. A neuroscientist named David Barack and his team made a video game that re-creates the experience of foraging for berries. Rewards are scattered through various patches, each with dwindling rewards. The player’s job is to figure out how long to stay at one patch before moving to another.

The kids with ADHD significantly outscored their non-ADHD peers on the game.

This evidence shows that we are looking at a distinct cognitive style – not a defect or a myth.

Why “Disorder” Is the Wrong Word

Why does the word “disorder” matter so much here?

Because “disorder” isn't a neutral description. It implies dysfunction — that something inside of you isn't working the way it should. That's why there's no such thing as “unwanted pregnancy disorder.”

The term “disorder” shares the same conceptual space as “disease,” and it has the same practical effect in the classroom: once you start using the word, you stop looking at the environment and start looking at the kid. You postulate hypothetical inner causes — executive functioning deficits, noradrenaline imbalances — to explain why the kid can't do what the others do.

What Comes Next

So what are the next steps?

First, people who’ve been diagnosed with ADHD, and their parents, need to fully understand their condition. There’s nothing wrong with their brain. They have a distinct cognitive style that doesn't match the demands placed on them. That frees us up to begin thinking about life paths – and educational systems – that would allow them to flourish rather than flounder.

Second, people need to know that there are non-medical interventions to shape their cognitive system. Four such commonsense interventions were described in The Great ADHD Myth? Less screen time. More time outdoors. Cutting out ultra-processed foods. Yoga.

It's notable that ADHD diagnosis rates in the U.S. run nearly triple those in France. Part of the reason is policy: European guidelines generally treat medication as a last resort, preferring techniques for managing attention over drugs.

Third, we need to change our educational system. Fortunately, this does not require a complete overhaul. Montessori and Waldorf schools have been doing this for decades by creating educational environments that prioritize flexible, hands-on discovery over classroom lectures. One concrete step: give kids with ADHD a voucher to attend one of these schools, rather than asking them to keep adapting to a system that was never built for how they think.

A version of this post appears in my Substack.

item.title: How Attachment Style Affects Your Health
item.description:
Attachment

How Attachment Style Affects Your Health

Your capacity for emotional intimacy matters.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Attachment theory is gaining prominence in the health care field.
  • Increasing evidence links attachment style to health and illness.
  • To boost your daily well-being, sustain a secure attachment style.

Do you feel in control of your physical health? It seems increasingly hard to know what's really effective, as popular newsfeeds tout the alleged benefits of obscure grains, mega-vitamin supplements, and exotic fitness methods like bathing or swimming in icy water. However, you're less likely to hear that your overall well-being is affected by your capacity to enjoy emotionally close relationships, such as those involving friendship, family ties, and romantic love: namely, your attachment style.

Of course, the notion that we're uplifted by gratifying social bonds isn't new. As Maslow's biographer, I discovered that he was influenced as early as the 1950s by such founders of psychosomatic medicine as psychiatrist Felix Deutsch. Initially serving as Sigmund Freud's personal physician in 1920s Vienna, Deutsch fled Nazi Germany and specialized in mind-body research upon coming to the United States. He and Maslow became friendly colleagues in the Boston area, though never actively collaborating. Partly through Deutsch's clinical studies with patients, Maslow became sure that medical science would eventually show that our social relationships in daily life greatly impact our overall well-being.

In The Farther Reaches of Human Nature, Maslow drew upon his influential hierarchy of inborn needs to assert: "The indications are [this is mostly extrapolation rather than hard data] that...increasing psychological health...can probably also increase [one's] longevity and reduce [one's] susceptibility to disease... The loss of the basic need satisfactions of safety and protection, belongingness, love, respect, self-esteem, identity, and self-actualization produces illnesses and deficiency diseases." To put it plainly, if we feel unsafe, lonely or isolated, unloved, disrespected, demeaned, ignored for our uniqueness, or thwarted in trying to fulfill our potentials, these unmet needs all have real consequences for our health.

Evidence From Attachment Theory

At the time of Maslow's sudden death in 1970, attachment theory hadn't yet arisen to bolster his viewpoint. Its originator was the British developmental psychologist-psychiatrist John Bowlby, who argued that humans are born with an innate drive to form a close bond with a primary caregiver, and that the first few years of life are crucial for its formation. Mary Ainsworth, a Canadian psychologist, expanded attachment theory to emphasize that, based on the subtleties of this bond, we develop an emotional structure that largely determines our lifelong capacity for emotional closeness with others. Later researchers refined attachment theory in recognition of cultural differences in child-rearing, but the basic paradigm is that everyone fits one of these four attachment styles: secure, anxious, avoidant, or disorganized ( "chaotic").

It's now clear that attachment style affects our health as early as adolescence. In a study led by Marjo Flykt in Finland, teenagers who felt insecure with their parents as well as peers had the highest levels of mental health problems and substance abuse. Contrastingly, those who felt secure in both sets of relationships had the lowest levels. Another intriguing finding: Secure attachment to parents seemed to specifically help teens manage their anger, whereas secure attachment to peers prevented internalizing problems like anxiety and depression.

Research consistently shows that adults, too, with an insecure attachment style (anxious, avoidant, or disorganized) have a weaker ability to regulate their emotions, including anger. In view of the clear link between chronic anger and cardiovascular disease, this finding has important health implications. Specifically, avoidant people overreact emotionally and physiologically while arguing, whereas their anxious counterparts become re-enraged and emotionally fixated when recalling past angry encounters. Those with secure attachment are much more likely to "forgive and forget" and, perhaps, have fewer regrets as they age.

Studies also reveal that insecure adults are more likely to suffer chronic pain—and experience it in more numerous bodily areas, compared to their securely attached peers. Why would this be? The explanation seems multifaceted: They have greater difficulty in regulating negative emotions, feel less social support from family members, and tend to "catastrophize" about their condition. Additionally, avoidant individuals are less likely to initiate affectionate touch, though they reap its benefits as much as others. In short, even the physiology of chronic pain has personality and social dimensions.

Boosting Our Attachment Security

Can we boost our attachment security? Increasingly, the scientific answer is yes. Therapeutic interventions focus on bolstering our feelings of safety—such as through guided imagery—by recalling a particular person or place that helped us feel secure. Known as attachment security priming, it seems consistent with Maslow's belief in the efficacy of actively remembering our peak experiences through expressive writing, artistic, or musical/dance activity.

item.title: Do Porn Users Seek More Extreme Content Over Time?
item.description:
Pornography

Do Porn Users Seek More Extreme Content Over Time?

Research challenges the idea that people build up a tolerance to violent porn.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • According to the content progression thesis, porn users seek more extreme content with continued use.
  • A two-year study tracked porn use and preferences in a sample of young men.
  • Preferences for violent and coercive content actually decreased across the study period.
  • These findings suggest that porn use doesn't lead to a tolerance effect.
Source: Photo by Charles Deluvio on Unsplash

Popular media articles often talk about pornography as if it has effects similar to those of drugs. Among other things, these reports claim that consumers build up a tolerance to porn over time, meaning that they eventually need to seek out increasingly extreme content in order to become aroused and/or to reach orgasm.

Researchers have dubbed this idea the content progression thesis and it has been discussed in the scientific literature for more than 30 years. During that time, a few small studies have emerged that provide support for it. However, all of those studies have suffered from the same limitation: People were only surveyed once and they were asked to report on how their pornography use had changed over time. Studies like this are subject to memory and recall biases, and they don’t allow us to make any inferences about cause and effect.

Testing the Content Progression Thesis

A study published in the journal Social Science Research aimed to address these limitations by using a longitudinal research design. With this kind of approach, researchers were able to document potential changes in patterns of porn use as they unfolded.

Scientists from the University of Zagreb in Croatia surveyed 248 male high-school students about their frequency of pornography use and porn preferences at five different points in time, each separated by about six months.

Participants were age 16 on average when the study began and they completed each phase of the survey online. The main questions of interest focused on how often they used porn in the past six months, as well as the extent to which they had a preference for porn with violent or sexually coercive content. Violent and coercive content were the focus here because that’s really where the main concern has been with the content progression thesis. The idea is that if porn users become desensitized, they may increasingly seek out violent content, potentially increasing demand for it and contributing to the normalization of sexual violence.

Do Porn Preferences Become More Extreme With Time?

So what did they find? First, pornography use in general remained pretty stable over the course of the study, with only a very slight trend toward more usage over time.

Second, and inconsistent with the content progression thesis, reported preferences for extreme content actually decreased during the study period. Specifically, whereas 8.1% of participants reported a preference for violent/coercive porn at the beginning of the study (the highest point), this dropped to 4.6% by the fourth data collection period (the lowest point).

The researchers also found that those who consumed porn more frequently at the beginning of the study showed a less marked decline in their preference for extreme content. This finding is neither consistent nor inconsistent with the content progression thesis, and the study authors believe that it simply reflects the fact that people who use porn more often tend to have more diverse interests and seek out a wider range of pornographic content.

What Can We Take Away From This Study?

Although this study is important because it tested the content progression thesis with a longitudinal research design, it does have its limitations. For example, the study only included young men, lasted just two years, and only inquired about violent/coercive porn. It would therefore be useful for future studies to examine potential effects in women and older adults, as well as to look for changes over a longer period of time and consider preferences for a wider range of “extreme” content.

That said, these results challenge the popular view that porn consumers necessarily build up a tolerance over time that encourages them to seek out increasingly violent content. These findings also cast doubt on the popular porn-as-a-drug analogy because “tolerance” doesn’t seem to be one of the hallmarks of the way that porn affects consumers.

item.title: The Biggest Mistake Overthinkers Make About Other People
item.description:
Anxiety

The Biggest Mistake Overthinkers Make About Other People

How to stop a guess from becoming an argument.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Catch the moment "maybe" becomes "definitely."
  • Calm down first and seek answers second.
  • Ask questions the other person can answer.

My wife and I had a little tiff a few days ago. Afterward, she playfully came up to me with a smile and said something that really sank in. She said, "Hon, if jumping to conclusions were an Olympic sport, you'd win the gold medal." After laughing, I realized she was right. A brief comment or delayed reply can send my mind racing (filling in the blanks) before I have even asked a single question. Looking at this further, I realized I start to replay that explanation until it feels less like a guess and more like evidence.

Overthinking Sends Us Jumping to Conclusions

I have battled overthinking — contending with those maddening, incessant thought loops — all of my life, and I can see how it has trained me to be a highly skilled jumper — that is, a jumper to conclusions. I also see how often the overthinking/jumping-to-conclusions pattern plays out in the struggles of children, teens, adult children, and parents. A child may think, "My friend didn't sit with me because they are mad at me." A spouse hearing a clipped response may think, "He's been angry at me all day." Or a parent whose adult child hasn't returned a text thinks, "She only wants to talk to me when she needs money."

While researching my recent book, When Overthinking Overtakes Your Child, I realized there are often kernels of truth in some overthinkers' interpretations. The big problems begin when we act as though we have confirmed something we overinterpret or misinterpret.

The Tricky Part of Overthinking

What makes overthinking so challenging is that, on the surface, it looks like careful reasoning. Yet it is often our attempt to escape the discomfort of not knowing. That emotional pain of sitting with ambiguity is what catapults us into maddening overthinking loops. Our minds fill in the blanks, and then we reflexively, often beyond our awareness, keep rehearsing the answer. By the time we speak, we may be arguing with a story our minds created that the other person has never heard.

Following are three ways to interrupt that tricky overthinking process that drives us to jump to conclusions.

1. Catch the Moment "Maybe" Becomes "Definitely"

Every week I have upset counseling and coaching clients express some version of "What did they mean by that?" Then they jump to those dreaded conclusions, way too fast: "Obviously, she was trying to hurt me." So, when you feel and hear yourself driving down the Jumping to Conclusions Expressway, take a pause and name what just happened. You might say to yourself, "Hey, I have an interpretation, but I don't have the whole story." You don't need to replace a frightening thought with a cheery one; you just need to leave room for information you don't have yet.

2. Calm Down First and Seek Answers Second

When we feel rejected or threatened, we can become unbelievably persuasive lawyers advocating for first interpretations. That's why, if you have read some of my past posts, I keep emphasizing two crucial life skills: calming down and solving problems. Interestingly, the same suggestion for children works for adults when it comes to overthinking and runaway thoughts. Before you send a charged text or deliver a pedantic speech, give yourself a few minutes, then ask, "What do I actually know firsthand, and what parts did I assume?"

3. Ask a Question the Other Person Can Answer

"You never call unless you need something" is a statement, and it invites a defense. Instead, try saying, "I'd like to hear from you more often. How does that feel to you?" Now the other person has room to tell you what's going on, rather than defend against the conclusion you jumped to. If their answer surprises you, that's a chance to learn something your first interpretation missed.

Final Thoughts

Of course, sometimes your first interpretation may be right. So, just know that taking a healthy pause doesn't mean dismissing your instincts. Rather, it means giving reality a chance to catch up with your instincts. My wife's joke landed because I saw myself in it. I'm still practicing, but the event I'd rather win (instead of jumping to conclusions) is the one where I stop at the edge, calmly ask a question, and don't jump.

item.title: Are You Leading a K-Shaped Organization?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Are You Leading a K-Shaped Organization?

Why some leaders see progress while others experience pain.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • In a K-shaped organization, what leaders believe and how people feel diverge during change.
  • Organizational pain in the form of frustration, friction, and fatigue rarely reach the top.
  • AI may widen the reality delta when interpretation begins to substitute for conversations with people.
  • Leaders can close the K by making hidden pain visible and acting on what they hear.

Economists use the term “K-shaped” to describe an economy in which some groups pull ahead while others fall behind. A similar divergence can take shape inside organizations—especially during periods of change.

Research on organizational silence and threat helps explain why. When employees believe speaking up is risky or futile, concerns are more likely to remain hidden (Morrison & Milliken, 2000). Under threat, people and organizations can narrow their attention and fall back on familiar routines (Staw, Sandelands, & Dutton, 1981). Over time, leaders and employees can begin to inhabit different experiences of the same change: Leaders become increasingly confident that progress is being made, while employees experience growing friction, anxiety, or fatigue.

That divergence can be pictured as a K. Before the change, the vertical stem represents a roughly shared reality about how work gets done. At the point of launch—a new system goes live, a restructuring is announced, or an AI tool is rolled out—the line splits into two branches. One reflects what leaders believe; the other reflects how people feel as they live through the change.

K-shaped Organizations
Source: Jeffrey Yip

The space between the upper and lower branches is what I call the reality delta—the gap between what leaders believe is happening and how people experience the change as they try to get work done (Yip, 2025b). In a K-shaped organization, the delta widens as the two branches move farther apart.

Understanding Organizational Pain

The lower branch is where organizational pain collects. I define organizational pain as the frustration, friction, and fatigue people experience when priorities, systems, or relationships get in the way of doing good work.

Pain can be emotional or structural. Emotional pain includes anxiety about the future, fear of losing competence or status, or the sting of feeling ignored. Structural pain is what the system does to people: conflicting priorities, tools that clash with the workflow, unclear roles, and messages that add noise without adding clarity.

If the pain is real, why do leaders miss it? One reason is that organizations are usually better at reporting the upper branch than the lower one. Dashboards capture adoption, deadlines, and outputs. They rarely capture hesitation, workaround fatigue, quiet anxiety, or what people say after the meeting. Over time, what is easiest to measure can start to feel like the whole reality.

Other factors:

Silence filters the bad news. Morrison and Milliken (2000) described how organizational silence develops when people conclude that speaking up is futile or risky. Problems then reach leaders softened, delayed, or not at all.

Competence hides the pain. Tucker and Edmondson (2003) studied hospital nurses who repeatedly encountered operational failures. Nurses often solved the immediate problem and kept the work moving. Their competence protected patients in the moment, but the workarounds also made broken systems less visible.

How AI May Widen the Reality Delta

AI can widen the reality delta when interpretation starts to replace conversation. Leaders can increasingly use AI to infer what people are thinking and feeling without speaking directly with them.

Recent research suggests a risk of sycophancy. Cheng and colleagues (2026) found that AI responses affirmed users’ actions more often than human responses; interacting with sycophantic AI also increased users’ confidence that they were right while reducing willingness to repair interpersonal conflict.

At the extreme, Hudon and Stip (2025) describe how sustained AI interactions may reinforce maladaptive or unusual beliefs in vulnerable users. The evidence does not show that ordinary AI use causes delusion, but the mechanism matters: AI may provide less corrective friction than conversations with people who see things differently.

For leaders, the everyday risk is simpler: What leaders believe may become more polished without becoming more grounded. AI should not replace the conversations that keep leaders close to reality; it should help leaders know which conversations to have.

Why the K Matters

Pain is information. When leaders can see it, pain can point to what needs to change. When pain is experienced primarily as threat, however, people and organizations can narrow their attention, centralize control, and fall back on familiar routines. Staw, Sandelands, and Dutton (1981) described this pattern as threat rigidity.

This suggests an important distinction: Pain that is acknowledged can guide adaptation, while pain that remains unheard can harden into rigidity, cynicism, or quiet withdrawal. From the top, the change may continue to look successful until adoption stalls, errors surface, or valued people leave. By then, the reality delta may be wide and costly to close.

There is also a counterintuitive implication: Healthier organizations may sometimes look worse before they look better. Edmondson (1996) found that hospital units with more open and supportive leadership reported more medication errors, not fewer.

Listen for Signals

In earlier work, I described four signals leaders can listen for when change is underway: Priorities, Anxiety, Inertia, and Noise, or PAIN (Yip, 2025a). Priorities show up when people are pulled in too many directions. Anxiety shows up in worries about competence, workload, or future roles. Inertia appears when old routines persist because the new way does not yet work well enough. Noise appears as confusion, overload, and competing messages.

The value of these signals is not in diagnosing employees but in helping leaders notice where the lived experience of change may be diverging from the official story.

The challenge is to learn to read both branches of the K. The PAIN framework offers four places to look for experiences that may not appear in formal reports. For each one, ask not only, "What are we seeing?" but "What might we be missing?"

Closing the K
Source: Jeffrey Yip

Closing the K

Closing the K means bringing what leaders believe closer to what people experience.

Use the PAIN framework as a practical K-check. Assess if the two branches are moving closer together or farther apart.

The upper branch is easier to see. The lower branch requires deliberate listening.

My challenge to you: Notice the pain in conversations, hesitation, workarounds, and silence.
